q: Burgundy's vineyards run predominantly along which orientation?
opts: South-facing slopes above a coastal plain
A chain of north-facing river valleys
A narrow escarpment facing broadly east
A wide plateau of even aspect facing west
exp: East-facing mid-slope catches the morning sun and drains well. In a marginal climate that aspect is the difference between ripe and not.

q: Red Burgundy from the Cote d'Or is made from which single variety?
exp: Burgundy is a region of monovarietal wines, which is what makes it the reference for expressing site: the grape is held constant and the vineyard varies.

q: White Burgundy, with rare exceptions, is made from which variety?
exp: Chardonnay is thought to have originated here, from a crossing of Pinot and Gouais Blanc, and Burgundy remains its benchmark.

q: Which secondary white grape has its own regional appellation in Burgundy?
exp: Bourgogne Aligote is a separate appellation. The grape is sharper and leaner than Chardonnay, and is the traditional base of a kir.

q: Gamay's expulsion from the Cote d'Or was ordered in the fourteenth century by whom?
exp: The 1395 edict of the Duke of Burgundy called it disloyal and drove it south. Whatever the politics, the result was to reserve the Cote d'Or for Pinot Noir.

q: Pinot Noir is notoriously difficult to grow. Which characteristic is most responsible?
opts: Very high tannin needing years to soften
exp: Thin skins give the pale colour and fine texture, and also the vulnerability. Tight clusters trap moisture and invite rot in a damp autumn.

q: Burgundy's appellation pyramid has how many broad tiers?
exp: Regional, Village, Premier Cru and Grand Cru. The tiers describe delimited land rather than the producer, which is the opposite of the Bordeaux chateau model.

q: Of every hundred bottles of Burgundy, roughly how many are Grand Cru?
exp: It is a tiny fraction of a small region, which is much of why the wines cost what they do. Regional appellations account for over half.

q: On a Grand Cru label from the Cote d'Or, what typically appears as the appellation?
exp: Chambertin and Montrachet stand on their own, without a village name. It is the clearest signal of the top tier on the label.

q: A Premier Cru wine is labelled how?
exp: Gevrey-Chambertin Clos Saint-Jacques, for example. The village comes first, which distinguishes it from a Grand Cru at a glance.

q: Many Cote d'Or villages appended the name of their finest vineyard in the nineteenth century. Which is an example?
exp: Gevrey took Chambertin, Chambolle took Musigny, Vosne took Romanee. Savigny's suffix points at the town of Beaune, not at a vineyard, and Pommard and Saint-Aubin appended nothing at all. It flatters the village and confuses the newcomer, permanently.

q: What does the Burgundian term climat denote?
opts: The weather of a given vintage
A cellar shared by the growers of one village
A cuvee blended from several parcels
exp: A named parcel whose boundaries and reputation are centuries old, not merely a plot of land. The climats were recognised by UNESCO in 2015.

q: Fragmentation of Burgundian vineyard ownership is largely attributable to what?
opts: Rules obliging growers to sell through a cooperative
exp: Equal division across generations split parcels into slivers, which is why one Grand Cru can have dozens of owners each making a different wine.

q: A negociant in Burgundy does what?
opts: Buys grapes or wine and bottles it under its own name
Exports finished wine but never bottles any itself
Sets the appellation boundaries for each village
Owns outright every vineyard whose wine it bottles
exp: A negociant may buy grapes, must or finished wine, and bottle it under its own name. Buying fruit lets a house work across many appellations. The distinction from a domaine, which bottles only its own fruit, is worth reading on the label.

q: Which Cote de Nuits village holds the greatest number of Grands Crus?
exp: Nine, headed by Chambertin and Chambertin-Clos de Beze. It is the largest of the Cote de Nuits communes as well.

q: Vosne-Romanee is celebrated above all for what?
opts: Producing the largest volume in Burgundy
A concentration of the most prized Grands Crus
exp: Romanee-Conti, La Tache, Richebourg and their neighbours sit within a few hundred metres of one another. It is the most expensive ground in wine.
